screens.description: The customer prepares to scan their biometric passport chip using an NFC-enabled phone.
The application reads the passport chip and displays the scanning progress.

knowledge.content: In Step 3, the customer holds their phone against their passport so the application can read its biometric chip using contactless NFC technology.

knowledge.topic: Why the Passport Chip Is Scanned
knowledge.content: The passport chip holds information that is used as part of the identity verification process. Scanning it helps confirm that the passport is genuine and belongs to the customer.

NFC stands for Near Field Communication. It allows compatible devices to communicate wirelessly over very short distances. The application uses NFC to read the electronic chip inside a biometric passport.
The prototype instructs the customer to target the passport back cover or photo page and hold their phone against the passport during scanning.
The NFC Ready indicator shows that the application is displaying a ready state for NFC scanning. The customer can select Start scan to begin.
The Start scan button begins the passport chip scanning process in the prototype.

The application displays Reading your passport while scanning is in progress. The customer should hold their phone against the passport and keep it still. The screen indicates that this may take a few seconds.
The prototype displays scanning progress and status indicators. These include MRZ Document Key decoded, Extracting biometric facial data, and Validating digital signature.

MRZ stands for Machine Readable Zone. It refers to the machine-readable information printed on a passport's identity page. Information from this zone can be used to derive a document access key for reading the electronic passport chip.

The prototype displays an Extracting biometric facial data stage. This represents reading facial biometric information stored in the electronic passport chip. It does not mean that the application has completed identity verification.

The prototype includes a digital signature validation stage. Digital signatures are used in electronic passports to help verify that chip data is authentic and has not been altered. The screen does not by itself confirm that the application has been approved.
During scanning, the screen instructs the customer to keep their phone still because the application is reading information from the passport chip.
The scanning screen includes a Cancel Scan button. This is intended to stop the current scanning attempt.

If scanning is unsuccessful, the customer can try again while holding the phone steady against the passport. If the problem continues, the customer can use Ask Sense to request guidance or ask for human assistance.

The prototype states that passport scanning may take a few seconds. If the scan appears stuck or repeatedly fails, the customer can request assistance rather than assuming that scanning has completed.
